clue.text: Exciting total one's charged for heating

parts.note: an exciting performance is described as electric
blanket as an adjective means total, covering everything, as in a blanket ban

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled by the sum they have been billed for heating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' looks like being billed, but it means electrically charged: the definition is a thing plugged in to warm a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated bedcover runs on mains current, so it is a device that is charged with electricity to give warmth.

clue.text: Rowling character shaving head and bottom, sparkling stuff in general

indicators.note: shaving cuts away the first and last letters of the name, its head and its bottom in a down entry

parts.note: Hagrid is the giant gamekeeper in J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter books
cola is a fizzy soft drink

explanation.surface: A Harry Potter giant being shaved, with talk of sparkling drinks thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shaving head and bottom' removes H and D from HAGRID, leaving AGRI. 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnaeus Julius Agricola was the Roman general who governed Britain, famous from the biography by his son-in-law Tacitus.

clue.text: A proportion of popular vote for Australian PM

indicators.note: proportion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A share of the electorate's ballots going to Australia's prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'for', which is only a link word; the definition is 'Australian PM'. PM is post meridiem, the afternoon, not Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang shortens afternoon to this word, and PM is the standard abbreviation for afternoon hours.

clue.text: Popular political veteran an insubstantial figure, according to Spooner?

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, signals that the starts of the two words trade places

parts.note: a bony figure is thin, without substance
ten is a number, a figure

explanation.surface: A well-liked elder statesman dismissed as a mere wisp of a man.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of BONY TEN gives the sound of the name; the second word is then spelt with a double N.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Benn was a long-serving and much-loved Labour politician in Britain, an MP for half a century.

clue.text: Mark, Athenian character shackling Turkish leader

indicators.note: shackling means holding something bound inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: sigma is a letter of the Greek alphabet, a character an Athenian would write

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A man called Mark, from Athens, putting a Turkish chief in chains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shackling' puts T, the first letter of 'Turkish', inside SIGMA. 'Mark' looks like a name but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace, and in botany or medicine also a visible spot or mark.

clue.text: Sex neither this nor that?

definitions.meaning: a coy British slang phrase for sexual intercourse
of three things, the one that is not this one and not that one

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about a sex that is neither one nor the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jokey euphemism for sex, and literally it names the remaining option once this and that are ruled out.

clue.text: Secure horses

definitions.meaning: firm and steady, not likely to fall
a group of racehorses kept by one trainer is called by the name of their building

explanation.surface: An instruction to lock up the horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady thing is secure; a racing yard's string of horses shares the name of the building they are kept in.

clue.text: Author writing about men — his weren't gay

indicators.note: about signals the letters are turned around and rearranged as the author writes them out anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A novelist whose male characters were known for being far from cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the anagram signal, with 'writing' as its run-in: the fifteen letters of MEN HIS WERENT GAY rearrange into the novelist's full name. 'gay' in its old sense means cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway was the American novelist of The Old Man and the Sea and A Farewell to Arms.

clue.text: Fancy rogue and tall yob

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamented, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dashing rascal who is also a tall thug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' is the anagram signal; ROGUE and TALL together give the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lager lout is a British name for a young man who gets drunk on beer and behaves aggressively, a yob.

clue.text: One despising another mad character half-heartedly

indicators.note: the heart of the word is its doubled middle letter, and half of that pair is dropped

parts.note: the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland, another madman after the earlier puzzle character

explanation.surface: Someone sneering at a different lunatic, though without much conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' removes one T of the middle TT of HATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who loathes or scorns something is one who hates it, so despising and hating are near synonyms.

clue.text: Herb that's trendy with duck wings on rosemary

parts.note: chic means fashionable, stylish
in cricket a duck is a score of nothing, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its two outer letters, one at each side

explanation.surface: A fashionable herb dish: duck wings served on a bed of rosemary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck' is a cricket score of zero, giving O; 'wings on rosemary' are R and Y. Duck wings and rosemary sound like a recipe, but they are wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicory is a blue-flowered plant whose leaves are eaten in salads and roots used as a coffee substitute, often classed as a herb.

clue.text: Word used in separation — "a snip", say?

indicators.note: say signals that the bargain phrase is spoken out loud, matching a word of parting

parts.note: in British English a snip is a bargain, a good buy

explanation.surface: A word spoken at a parting, perhaps a cut being made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a snip' looks like cutting, fitting 'separation', but it is British slang for a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: People say this farewell when they part from one another, so it is the word used at a separation.

clue.text: Con man

explanation.definitionFit: To cheat someone out of money is to fleece or swindle them, and the castle is one of the pieces in chess.

clue.text: Unit chatted about outstanding soldiers

indicators.note: read as out-standing: the rearranged letters stand outside the next piece
about signals the letters of the word chatted are turned around into a new order

parts.note: men is a common crossword word for soldiers, especially other ranks

explanation.surface: A unit gossiping about soldiers who are excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges the gossip word into DETACHT; 'outstanding' is read as standing outside, so those letters go round the soldiers to give DETACH-MEN-T.
explanation.definitionFit: A detachment is a group of troops sent away from the main body on a particular task, a military unit.

clue.text: Make roughly a hundred rowers minus a thousand

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: minus means take away, so one letter is removed from the rowers

parts.note: oarsmen are people who row
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Instructions to build something crudely from about a hundred rowers less a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' looks like 'approximately' beside 'a hundred', but it belongs with 'Make': make rough.
explanation.definitionFit: To coarsen something is to render it rough or crude, so the verb means to make a thing rough.

clue.text: Crush something underfoot — hurry up!

definitions.meaning: literally to tread on a thing
an informal order to go faster, from stepping on a car's accelerator

explanation.definitionFit: Treading on an object squashes it, and urging a driver to press the pedal harder means speed up.

clue.text: Fish to eat by river while lying back

indicators.note: by means beside, so the river letter sits next to the eating word
lying back has the word for while laid out in the opposite direction

parts.note: as can mean while, at the time that
R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps
to dine is to eat a meal

explanation.surface: Eating a meal on the riverbank while reclining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying back' is the reversal signal: the short word for while is laid backwards to open the answer. 'Fish' looks like a verb but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sardine is a small oily sea fish of the herring family, often sold tinned.

clue.text: Hygienic topless bar — madness?

indicators.note: the question mark tells the solver to read the madness word as in plus sanity, so a piece goes inside

parts.note: madness is insanity, which split as in-sanity gives the word for soundness of mind with something in it

indicators.note: topless means the bar loses its top, its first letter

parts.note: taken as the word itself, a pub counter

explanation.surface: Is it crazy for a bar with topless staff to call itself clean?
explanation.walkthrough: Think of insanity for 'madness', then split it as in-sanity: one word does double duty, naming the outer word and saying something goes inside it. The question mark flags this stretch; many solvers think it unfair.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanitary conditions are clean and free of germs, so the word means hygienic.

clue.text: Poisonous jerks lie in bed

indicators.note: jerks means moves with sudden twitches, so the letters are jolted out of place

explanation.surface: A poisoned person twitching while lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jerks' is the anagram signal for LIE IN BED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something poisonous cannot be eaten safely, which is one sense of inedible, unfit to be eaten.

clue.text: University on the border studying speech

indicators.note: on means placed after in an across clue, so the university follows the border word

parts.note: a lip is a rim or edge, a border
Reading is an English town with a well-known university

explanation.surface: A university situated on a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: READING is a university town west of London. 'studying speech' looks like a course at that university, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Deaf people follow what is said by watching mouth movements, a way of studying speech as it happens.

clue.text: Work having arisen, duck into internet meeting

indicators.note: arisen means gone up, and in a down entry the word for work reads upwards

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: into means the duck letter is placed inside the internet letters

parts.note: www stands for the World Wide Web
a duck in cricket is a zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Once a job is up, someone dodges into an online meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having arisen' reads the work word upwards to PO; 'into' puts the duck inside the web letters, giving WWOW. 'duck' looks like dodging but is the cricket score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A powwow is an informal word for a meeting or discussion, taken from a Native American gathering.

clue.text: Antelope bringing up a couple of children

indicators.note: bringing up in a down entry lifts the letters so they read from the bottom
a couple means two, so the child word appears twice

parts.note: a kid is a child

explanation.surface: An antelope raising a pair of youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a couple of' doubles KID; 'bringing up' turns KIDKID round. 'bringing up' looks like child-rearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dik-dik is a tiny African antelope, standing about a foot tall at the shoulder.

clue.text: Half of house missed

indicators.note: half of says a part of the following words is taken, here the tail of one word joined to the head of the next

explanation.surface: Part of the house was left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the end of 'house' and the start of 'missed', and the result is itself half of a pair of houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi is a semi-detached house, one of two homes sharing a wall, so it is half of a house.

clue.text: A city doubled in number?

parts.note: a number is a song, and a famous song repeats the name of this city twice in its title

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a city whose population has doubled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' looks like population size, but it is a song: the Sinatra hit names the city twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The song New York, New York, made famous by Frank Sinatra and Liza Minnelli, says the city's name twice in its title.

clue.text: Carol, after a drink, flirting

indicators.note: after means the carol word comes later, following the drink

parts.note: tea is a drink
to carol is to sing joyfully

explanation.surface: Carol, a woman, flirting after she has had a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name but is the verb to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Teasing someone playfully, with banter, is a way of flirting with them.

clue.text: A capital's musicians on top

parts.note: the LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra, musicians of the capital

explanation.surface: A city's musicians who are top of their field.
explanation.definitionFit: On top in the sense of in addition, besides, is a synonym for as well.

clue.text: Company crushed by priest, a sickener

indicators.note: crushed by means squeezed in by, so the company letters sit inside the priest

parts.note: Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A firm brought down by a clergyman who makes people ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crushed by' looks like a defeat, but it is the container signal: the priest's letters squeeze round the company. Eli is the Old Testament priest who taught Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: E. coli is a bacterium whose harmful strains cause food poisoning, something that makes people ill.

clue.text: A risible dickhead floundering as Mandela interpreter

indicators.note: floundering means struggling clumsily, so the letters flail into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
read as dick-head, the head of the word dick, its first letter

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a laughable fool who flounders while impersonating Mandela.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dickhead' looks like a crude insult, but it means the first letter of 'dick'. That D joins A RISIBLE, and 'floundering' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Idris Elba played Nelson Mandela in the 2013 film Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom, so he is an interpreter of the role.
